query_text: Are there any academic fields that don't have enough people trying to teach?

action.query: teacher shortage subject areas United States 2025 2026 academic fields
queries: teacher shortage subject areas United States 2025 2026 academic fields
AAEE educator supply and demand report 2025 subject shortage areas
US Department of Education teacher shortage areas 2025 2026

annotations.title: Teacher Shortage Areas | U.S. Department of Education
Teacher Shortages by Subjects Across States | Learning Policy Institute

content.text:
Yes. If you mean **K–12 / secondary-school teaching**, there are several academic subject areas in the U.S. that often don’t have enough qualified people trying to teach them. The exact shortages vary a lot by **state, district, grade level, and certification**, but the recurring shortage areas are:

- **Special education** — often the biggest and most persistent shortage.
- **Math**, especially middle and high school.
- **Science**, especially physics, chemistry, and sometimes biology.
- **Career and technical education** — trades, health sciences, business, agriculture, computer/IT, etc.
- **World languages** — Spanish is common, but shortages can be sharper in less commonly taught languages.
- **English as a Second Language / bilingual education**.
- **Computer science / technology education** in many places.
- **School support roles** like speech-language pathology, school psychology, counseling, and related services, though these are not always “academic fields” in the narrow sense.

The U.S. Department of Education maintains official state-designated teacher-shortage areas, and its examples include mathematics, science, foreign languages, bilingual education, and other fields states identify as short on qualified teachers. ([ed.gov](https://www.ed.gov/teaching-and-administration/professional-development/teacher-shortage-areas?utm_source=openai)) A 2025 Learning Policy Institute analysis also found widespread shortages across states, with many positions either vacant or filled by people not fully certified for their assignments. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-shortages-subjects-across-states-factsheet?utm_source=openai))

Fields that are **less likely** to have shortages, depending on location, often include **social studies/history, elementary education, English language arts, art, and physical education**—but that is not universal. Some rural districts, high-poverty districts, and certain states may still struggle to hire in those areas.

If you mean **college/university professors**, the picture is different: many academic disciplines actually have **more PhDs than tenure-track jobs**, especially in the humanities. Shortages are more likely in fields where people can earn much more outside academia, such as **nursing, accounting, computer science, engineering, data science, cybersecurity, and some health professions**.
